title: Water uptake and xerophytes; Adaptations
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX12#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX12#t4 term and clue written for the game; EX12#t1 term and clue written for the game; EX12#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EV09#N.3, EX12#N.2, EV09#N.18, EX12#N.9, EX12#N.15a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Hinge cells
items.clue: In marram grass these lose water in dry wind, so the leaf rolls up.

items.label: Spines
items.clue: What cactus leaves are reduced to, giving less surface for water loss.

items.label: Xerophyte
items.clue: Plant adapted to a dry habitat; it cannot stop water loss, so it reduces it.

items.label: Sunken stomata
items.clue: Pores lying in pits, so humid air is trapped and the gradient for water loss is smaller.

options.text: A rattlesnake's venom is an anatomical adaptation, because it is delivered through the fangs.
Zebras living in herds is not an adaptation, because behaviour is not inherited.
A kangaroo rat producing very concentrated urine is a physiological adaptation.
A dog moved to a cold country growing a thicker coat during its life is an anatomical adaptation.

questions.explanation: It is a body process, carried out by the kidneys, that saves water in the desert.

questions.stem: In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous root, where are the xylem and the phloem found?

options.text: In separate vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the outside of the root, in just the same way as in the stem.
At the centre of the root, with the xylem forming a star shape and groups of phloem between its arms.
At the centre of the root, with phloem forming a star shape and xylem in groups between its arms.
Spread throughout the cortex, which conducts water and sugars across the width of the root.

questions.explanation: The dicotyledonous root has a central vascular cylinder: xylem forms a star or cross shape in the middle and phloem lies in separate groups between the arms of the xylem. This is surrounded by the cortex and then the epidermis bearing root hairs.

questions.stem: Arctic foxes have much smaller ears than fennec foxes. Which statement best explains how small ears became typical of Arctic foxes?

options.text: Each Arctic fox's ears shrank during its life in the cold, and its cubs inherited the smaller ears.
Foxes with alleles for smaller ears lost less heat, so survived and bred more; the alleles spread.
The cold caused new mutations for small ears to arise in the foxes that needed them.
Small ears are better in every environment, so in time all foxes will evolve them.

questions.stem: A cut stem of a well-watered plant exudes sap from the xylem for several hours. When the roots are treated with a respiratory inhibitor, the exudation stops. What does this show about how the sap was being pushed out?

options.text: Root cells were actively transporting water into the xylem, and this active transport of water molecules needs ATP from respiration.
The exudation was caused by tension pulling water up the xylem, and the inhibitor stopped the transpiration that generates it.
The xylem vessels themselves were using ATP from respiration to push the sap upwards, and the inhibitor stopped them.
Root cells were using ATP to pump mineral ions into the xylem, so water entered by osmosis and produced a positive pressure.

questions.stem: A gardener scatters a large amount of fertiliser on dry soil around a plant. Within a day the plant wilts, although the soil has not dried further. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Root hair cells take in water whenever the plant needs it, so the wilting must have started in the leaves.
The fertiliser ions poisoned the pumps that actively transport water molecules into the root hairs.
The ions lowered the soil's water potential below the root hair cells', so water stopped entering by osmosis.
The ions raised the soil water's potential, so water drained away from the roots faster than it could be absorbed.
